subject: Biology
title: How Plants Drink: Water Transport
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: How Plants Drink: Water Transport.

hook.text: A tall tree moves hundreds of liters of water from its roots to its leaves every day—with no pump.

buildup.text: Water enters through root hairs by osmosis and travels up through xylem tubes.

discovery.text: Transpiration—water evaporating from leaf pores—creates a pulling force that draws water upward.

twist.text: Water molecules stick to each other through cohesion, forming an unbroken chain from root to leaf.

climax.text: This system lifts water over 100 meters in the tallest trees—defying gravity without muscles.

punchline.text: No heart, no pump. Just physics and biology.

quiz.question: What force pulls water up through a tree?

details.summary: Plants transport water from roots to leaves through xylem vessels using transpiration pull, the cohesion-tension mechanism. As water evaporates from leaf stomata, it creates negative pressure that pulls a continuous column of water upward, reaching heights exceeding 100 meters in tall trees.
details.whyItMatters: Water transport limits plant height and distribution. Understanding this system explains why forests need rain, why droughts kill trees, and how plants will respond to climate change affecting water availability worldwide.
takeaways: Transpiration pull draws water upward as it evaporates from leaf stomata
Cohesion between water molecules maintains an unbroken column in the xylem
A large oak tree can transpire over 400 liters of water per day

faq.question: How can water reach the top of a 100-meter tree without a pump?
faq.answer: As water evaporates from leaves, it creates negative pressure that pulls the continuous water column upward through xylem. Hydrogen bonds between water molecules maintain cohesion, and adhesion to xylem walls prevents the column from breaking. No metabolic energy pump is needed.

faq.question: Why do plants wilt when they do not get enough water?
faq.answer: Water provides turgor pressure that keeps plant cells rigid and stems upright. When water loss through transpiration exceeds uptake from roots, cells lose turgor and become flaccid. Wilting reduces leaf surface area exposed to sun, helping conserve remaining water.
